newsitem.title: MALTA: FEATURE - Europe's anti-divorce outpost under fresh attack.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Europe's anti-divorce outpost under fresh attack.

text.p: Pro-divorce activists in this staunchly Catholic country are mobilising to back the new prime minister's determination to introduce divorce to the Mediterranean island.

Less than a month after Prime Minister Alfred Sant dropped a bombshell on the country by declaring divorce should, and would, be introduced, activists early in March set up a Malta Divorce Movement to produce a divorce bill to go to Sant.

Its chairman Emmy Bezzina, a lawyer specialising in family matters, said: "We are studying legislation in France, Italy, Germany, the United Kingdom and other countries. We will seek a formal meeting with Dr Sant when the bill is ready."
Increasing numbers of separations, illegitimate children, co-habitation and single parenting all contribute to the social need for divorce, Bezzina said.
With Ireland now about to allow divorce, Malta would be the only country in Europe where divorce is not allowed.
SANT TELLS STUDENTS OF NEED FOR DIVORCE
Sant told a University student meeting last month that Malta needed provision for divorce, and national consensus had to be sought on the issue.
He planned to set up a commission later this year to study the problem and the government would wait for its report before deciding on its next step.
Malta is one of the most staunchly Roman Catholic countries in Europe, with churches always full for Sunday services.
Nearly all Maltese have elaborate church weddings -- there were 2,600 last year -- but calls for divorce have started appearing in the press as the number of separations increases.
Justice Minister Charles Mangion said in parliament that 900 cases for separation were filed in Maltese courts last year. Those couples were married over several years.
As separation cases are not filed jointly by husband and wife it was not clear whether the number involved 900 couples or 450.
Many Maltese argue that the absence of divorce is forcing people whose marriage has broken down to cohabitation, with their offspring facing many legal problems.
Besides stiff opposition to divorce from the church, the opposition Nationalist Party, toppled from government in elections on October 26, is against divorce.
His party still enjoys the support of 48 per cent of the electorate.
Opposition leader Eddie Fenech Adami has long spoken out against divorce, saying he hoped Malta would never reach the stage of needing to introduce it.

He told the same student forum that divorce was "an opportunity to have another partner with the approval of the law". He added that "laws should reflect the social conscience of the country, and Malta should not take the attitude that divorce should be introduced because it has been introduced in all other European countries."
OPPONENTS DENY GOVERNMENT MANDATE

Opponents of divorce argue that the government does not have the mandate to introduce it. Divorce was seen before the elections as too contentious to be included in any electoral programme, given the influence of the church.
Sant however had made known he personally favoured divorce although his Labour Party had no stand over the matter.
The only political party to have proposed the introduction of divorce in its electoral programme was the tiny Alternattiva Demokratika, which failed to elect anyone.

Helena Dalli, junior minister for women's rights, said she looked forward to the commission's recommendations. She was concerned, she said, about the plight of people whose marriage had broken down or who were in a relationship with separated partners.

"Separated people can only enter relationships which can never be regulated by law. Children born out of those relationships are the innocent victims of the way society regulates its affairs," she said.
Both Sant and Fenech Adami agree that divorce should not be the subject of a referendum.
"This is a case," Sant told the forum, "where the majority should not impose its beliefs on the minority."
